I have ADHD (diagnosed from neuropsychological testing done as a child and retesting as an adult, each lasting for ~8 hours and done by neuropsychologists). I see this same phenomenon online when it comes to ADHD.

It’s beyond infuriating how often people on social media talk about their “ADHD” symptoms like forgetting where they put their keys, their preferences for being on their phone instead of doing a task they’re dreading, getting energized when they’re excited, or restless in lengthy and boring meetings. These are all normal human experiences. EVERYONE does this.

But there is all this narrative about “adult onset ADHD” (which isn’t a thing) and how every person who is otherwise very successful but occasionally forgets they had an appointment or an item off their shopping list must be “masking”.

And then of course others read this and think, “hey I do this” and think they have ADHD. It does not help that so many family doctors hand out prescriptions based on them answering a few questions where the answer is obvious. There’s even online businesses that will diagnose someone and send them meds in an ongoing subscription model. Others don’t even bother with this low bar and claim to be self-diagnosed.

They treat ADHD as a quirky trait, when in reality living with the disorder is hell. I hate having ADHD so much, and I cannot stand when people trivialize it. The online ADHD discourse is doing so much damage to a disorder that’s already hugely misunderstood.

This morning I was cleaning out the litter box which we keep in a closet in the bathroom.  While I have the bathroom door partially opened and scooping up litter, Joey was in the bathroom with me. He wanted to get out of the bathroom, so he takes his front paw and smacks me on the leg (no claws, just the paw) as if he was saying "Hey lady, move it.  I want to get out."  The moment I moved my leg, he ran out.

Funny cat.  Every day he seems to find new ways to communicate with me and make me laugh.  Since I retired June 1st, his personality continues to change - for the better. They were few and far between, but had a lasting authenticity about them.

I didn’t pursue a conventional dream. This has a social cost, amongst other penalties. The best way to avoid being a jerk, I found, was not be lulled into joining the rat race. And not wanting to be a sucker demanded some street smarts, that is, understanding how the world actually worked and setting boundaries.

Both of these required some acceptance of being one among many. It’s hard to stay grounded when the world always seems to be selling you something. But there are extraordinary delights in an ordinary life. None of this is easy and straightforward, but it’s been worth it.

The Houthis were the target of six invasions of Saada Governate (Province) by the Yemeni Army of authoritarian Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh from 2004 to 2010 (collectively known as the Saada Wars).  In each invasion, the Houthis gained more military competence until the final 2010 invasion when the Houthis decisively defeated the Yemeni Army.  Iranian support of the Houthis began in the later stages of this conflict, and has consisted primarily of providing the Houthis with a long-range strike capability in the form of drones and cruise and ballistic missiles.  Hezbollah has also provided the Houthis with a model for revolutionary ideology and bureaucratic organization. comments.name: Neil
comments.body:
Oh, now this is a lovely piece.

Ms. Phillips tells us something right off which is obscured in most reactions to this latest movie version of the Odyssey: There is no "original" text, no book by Homer. This story is an oral tradition--like Paul Bunyan or Johnny Appleseed or John Henry--and it has many authors, and depending on who is "adapting" the story, the characters change.

Personally, I love Marie Phillips' version of the Greek gods behaving badly, but that's just me. The image of Aphrodite working in a London phone sex enterprise is just priceless.

But Circe, for me, has shifted as I grew older: now she is more a goddess whose powers do not fulfill her; she is vulnerable to the strengths of Odysseus , capable of being enthralled, offering a mortal immortality to have her man. And yet, she is willing to release him. 

Ms. Phillips is likely correct: The "tell" in any rendition of the Odyssey is the depiction of Circe.

comments.body: This is a terribly simplistic and misguided read. Morton basically steals the film with her complex performance. Her defiance and mastery feel earned and authentic. Yes, Nolan totally elides the original's depiction of Odysseus distracted for a year by this powerful and alluring woman. But this does nothing to limit the impression Morton makes as a Circe in command of an environment hostile to her as a woman and as a civilian. Phillips also misses entirely the central role Calypso plays in Nolan's take - she effectively serves as a caregiver who brings Odysseus slowly back to strength enough to tolerate and remedy his memories of trauma. It's a bit woo-woo for me, but strengthening the hero until he can reckon with his experience in war hardly seems like a minor task. If Calypso had been a man I'm sure his care would be honored differently. Perhaps Phillips could benefit from questioning some of her own assumptions about what work is valuable.

This is a perennial subject of fascination for the NYT.   The implicit assumption is that your body balance of water is dependent on what you drink, and that only with careful conscious calculation and diligence can you keep your body in balance.   This ignores the fact that fluid and water balance is a problem that has been present for hundreds of millions of years, more critical even since coming out onto land, and that the kidney and brainstem have been working on it under penalty of death (or non-reproduction). 

This is a bit like reading a article about how to "breathe right" while ignoring the fact that you have a brainstem that is managing this all the time. 

Fortunately, it is not up to your cerebral cortex to have to mange this, for 95% of people.  If you drink a reasonable amount of fluids, your kidney and ancient brain will figure it out.    I doubt that any other animal on the planet is spending even a moment figuring out how much to drink and whether their diet is "hydrating" enough, yet somehow they seem OK. The same happens with thirst.  When your body needs hydration, hydration will be the ONLY thing your body thinks about after breathing.  Every moment you spend will be to find water.

You'll know you're hydrated enough when your body isn't sending you signals to seek out water.  It's that simple.

comments.name: Jaganathan
comments.body:
The devastating heatwaves currently fracturing Europe are a grim demonstration of climate change as a systems-level crisis where history, infrastructure, and human biology collide. There is a profound, tragic irony unfolding here: while the Global South is often forced into a carbon-heavy trap by an immediate infrastructural necessity to use cheap fossil fuels, Europe is now reaping the atmospheric whirlwind of the West’s historical emission legacy.
The current crisis proves that no amount of wealth creates a shield against a warped planet. Through El Niño teleconnections, a thermal anomaly thousands of miles away in the Pacific has distorted the jet stream, pinning a lethal, compressed heat dome directly over European cities.
This is where the historical infrastructure trap springs shut on Europe itself. For centuries, European buildings were engineered exclusively to retain heat, not repel it. When temperatures breach 37°C, these insulated structures become urban ovens. Stripped of the melanin shield that their ancestors evolutionary shed to survive in a low-sunlight environment, these unacclimatized populations face rapid, systemic physiological failure. The thousands of excess deaths recorded this summer are the direct result of an evolutionary and structural paradigm failing in real time. The infrastructure divide hasn't just left the developing world vulnerable; it has rendered the developed world an architectural trap.

20 years ago Stanford and places in Japan had technology addiction programs; kept quiet here because there were billions to be made.

As a communications professional and leadership/personal development coach, I began writing about the impact of technology 18 years ago...people thought I was crazy.

You did not need to be an "expert" or a scientist to see the addictive nature of technology and with it, social media. You just needed your common sense.

(And you needed to be willing to spend significant periods of time each day...separated from technology.)

Therein lies the problem; too much time spent on technology begins to limit our awarenesses, our common sense, oour critical thinking, our creativity and productivity.

The energy buzz you get from technology - your emotional and mental functions resonating with the speed of the internet - makes you "feel" like you are productive, but in fact, how could your real life productivity be better...when you are spending more and more time on technology?

The bottom line is this...

Life is about experience, real life experiences...within ourselves as a result of our contact and connection with others and with the world around us.

Time spent on technology takes time away from...real life experience.

Experience is the seed bed that cultivates wisdom, connection, creativity, empathy...and healthy relationships.

The "tool" of technology has become our master. Now, we must learn to use it in moderation and get back to real life.

comments.body: The bearding is not because there are so many bees but because it's so hot out. Just as New Yorkers would sit on the stoop (before air conditioning), bees move out of the hive when it's too hot inside. They're removing their own heat, making space for ventilation to cool the hive, and helping with ventilation by beating their wings and moving air into and out of the entrance. Workers actually carry water to the hive and then evaporate it by beating their wings. Honeybees invented evaporative cooling! After the hive cools down, they'll all move back inside.

I didn't plan this, so I guess it's synchronicity in action.

Kaplan's thesis is that the most difficult decision making for leaders involves when they must choose not between good versus evil, but between good versus good, and how it helps to have a sense of tragedy. It echoes unmistakably in how Rhaenyra’s well meaning decisions lead to death, rape, starvation, petty tyranny, and not so petty tyranny. And the most sickening aspects of it is how easily I can imagine myself making the same mistakes.

comments.body: It is an interesting idea, and I certainly agree that an extreme correction to the credo that AI is inevitable and can't be limited in anyway is warranted, however from my experience those who are 40+ have been often more susceptible to the harms of AI than younger people. For whatever reason, AI is one of those technologies that middle age to older people place a lot of faith in and have adopted much more quickly than others. The people I know who use AI for therapy and/or trust its life advice uncritically are primarily older than 40! So, if we are to go towards an extreme correction, I think the better correction is to pass laws that show direct hostility to it. Ban construction on new data centers for a year, remove Section 230 immunity specifically for AI generated content/responses, require all AI generated media to have a watermark, and hold AI companies strictly liable for any environmental damage they cause. I think these laws would send a clearer message that nothing is inevitable, people don't have to suffer for the "future," and that AI is more of a tool that can be limited like anything else.

The two important things to keep in mind is that use of AI is inevitable and will spread, and that its control by profit oriented companies will make the outcome worse than it could otherwise be.  Some mix of public access, regulation, and young people figuring out what really works is the key to a positive outcome for the interaction between humans and AIs.  Older people like myself, with a nostalgia for familiar ways of doing things, are not the ones who will come up with the solutions.

As a writer who uses AI regularly, I endorse this section of the author's opinion: "for a mature person, A.I. can be useful. A formed mind can argue or wrangle with the machine, reject its false polish and recognize when the language it constructs to redescribe the world has become too smooth or soulless. Someone who has lived with words long enough can sense when a sentence has not been earned, and someone who has already developed a voice can use the machine without allowing the machine to become the voice." This is exactly how I use AI. I've also learned to recognize the verbal tics that AI falls back on.

The author's own phrases — "earned," "allowing the machine to become the voice," "less like a tool and more like wisdom" — have exactly the smooth, false-polish quality she's warning against. It's the kind of language I now have to scrub out of my own drafts. Whether or not she used AI, the resemblance suggests we're all starting to write a little like AI

Some advice: watch out for words like "earned," "landed," and "unpack." And be wary of balance and antithesis that AI leans on so heavily. And full disclosure: yes, I did have Claude help me clean up this comment. .
